claims.text: The induction-melted Al–Mg–Cu–Zn–Gd alloy is initially a non-equilibrium high-entropy alloy.
The as-cast alloy consists predominantly of a metastable solid solution with a minor fraction of precursor intermetallic phases.
Isothermal annealing at 400–500 °C transforms the metastable solid solution into a microstructure containing a higher volume fraction of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
The annealing-induced Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates are finely dispersed in the matrix and along grain boundaries.
Thermal activation during annealing drives Mg diffusion and segregation.
Mg diffusion and segregation convert the metastable solid solution into a structure enriched in stable intermetallic compounds.
The Mg-rich precipitates create local chemical environments that favor nucleation and growth of a continuous, uniform, and adherent MgO scale during oxidation at 700–900 °C.
The MgO scale produced in the annealed condition is protective during high-temperature oxidation.
Formation of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates reduces compositional inhomogeneity.
Reduced compositional inhomogeneity mitigates galvanic corrosion in 3.5% NaCl at room temperature.
Annealed samples will have a statistically significant increase in Mg-rich intermetallic content relative to the as-cast baseline.
Annealed samples will form a more uniform and adherent MgO scale than as-cast samples under high-temperature oxidation.
Annealed samples will exhibit lower corrosion current density than as-cast samples in 3.5% NaCl.
The proposed mechanism applies when alloy density is below 6 g/cm3 and processing limits excessive grain growth.
